newsitem.title: UK: UK Sept Purchasing Managers' (PMI) survey - Text.
newsitem.headline: UK Sept Purchasing Managers' (PMI) survey - Text.

text.p: Following is a full text of the September report on Business of the Chartered Institutue of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS)
OUTPUT AND NEW ORDERS BUOYANT. DELIVERY TIMES STAY GOOD AND PRICES REMAIN WEAK.

The manufacturing economy continued to pull out of the slowdown experienced throughout last year and the first half of this year. The Purchasing Managers' Index for September signalled the fourth successive monthly increase in manufacturing activity and rose to the highest level recorded for seventeen months. Both output and new order levels recorded the largest monthly increases since the Autumn of 1994 while the quantity of inputs bought by companies showed the first significant monthly increase since April last year.

The main source of the increase in demand continued to be UK markets. In particular, demand has largely stemmed from rising levels of consumers' expenditure, which has expanded order books and driven up output levels in firms producing consumer goods.

In recent months this growth has filtered down to producers who supply components to the consumer sector. In September growth appears to have filtered down a further level, to producers of investment goods such as plant and machinery. These latter producers saw their first significant increase in new orders for a year as companies increased their capital expenditures in order to expand.

However, although investment in plant and machinery appears to have risen, companies remained reluctant to take on more staff. Roughly the same proportion of companies surveyed reported a decrease in staffing levels as reported an increase.
The lack of recruitment was in part explained by the slow growth of export orders which, although rising modestly, continued to be restrained by slow economic growth in European markets.

This weakness of world-wide demand continued to influence input prices, which fell again. However, the number of companies reporting a fall in prices dropped to its lowest since January, causing the Prices index to move upwards for the second consecutive month. This was linked to the steady improvement in demand which has made suppliers busier. Lead-times the shortening of which indicates the existence of spare capacity have shown no significant change for the past two months. Firms have increasingly had to meet demand through higher output rather than from the warehouse shelf.

* The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of activity in the manufacturing economy and acts as a leading indicator for the whole economy. The indicator is derived from individual diffusion indices which measure changes in output, new orders, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of goods purchased. A reading of the PMI below 50% indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally declining; above 50%, that it is generally expanding. The seasonally adjusted index may be subject to revision as improved estimation of seasonal adjustments occur with each month's new data.
OUTPUT

The seasonally adjusted Output Index rose to the highest level recorded (therefore indicating the fastest rate of growth) since November 1994. Production of consumer goods showed especially strong growth in response to rising order levels, with suppliers of intermediate goods benefiting from the consumer sector expansion. Meanwhile, production of capital/investment goods also showed a welcome return to growth.
NEW ORDERS

The New Orders Index rose to its highest level since October 1994 and signalled an increase in the rate of growth. The primary source of new orders was the domestic market, with demand for consumer goods showing particular strength (although the index was also boosted by the first rise in orders for investment goods since August last year). New export orders rose modestly but were again restricted by slow growth in Europe.
QUANTITY OF PURCHASES

September saw the first significant increase in the amount of goods purchased by panel members since April 1995. Although purchasing activity has risen in the consumer industries over recent months to meet output expansion, September saw the first increase in purchasing within the investment and intermediate goods industries since late last year.
PRICES

The Prices Index moved upwards for the second month running but remained below 50.0 and thus signalled a further fall in prices. The rise in the index merely suggests that prices fell at a slower pace than the fast rate seen in the previous three months. Nearly 20% of firms saw prices fall against 6% who saw a rise. Worldwide demand remained weak by historical standards, especially for commodities, driving price competition.
SUPPLIERS' DELIVERY TIMES

The Suppliers' Delivery Times Index fell very marginally to 50.1, its lowest level since September last year. This level, not significantly higher than 50.0, indicates no overall change in the average length of delivery times. Suppliers of some products were reported to have become busier as purchasing managers increased their production requirements, but overall manufacturers continued to operate at levels well within capacity.
STOCKS OF PURCHASES

Although the amount of materials purchased rose in September, stocks of purchases were depleted through high usage in production. Good availability of supply for most materials, combined with widespread price competition among suppliers, continued to encourage purchasing managers to run stock levels as efficiently as possible.
STOCKS OF FINISHED GOODS

Producers of consumer goods increased their finished goods stock levels for the second month running to meet forecast demand. Destocking remained prevalent in the other sectors, however, in order to reduce costs. Producers of intermediate goods saw a particularly sharp fall in stocks as destocking policies were often accompanied by higher than expected sales (especially from customers in the consumer industries).
EMPLOYMENT

The Employment Index rose only marginally in September, indicating a broadly flat picture. Although the percentage of companies reporting higher employment rose, so did the percentage reporting lower employment. Companies remained concerned about recruitment of permanent staff. This was reflected in the fact that a fifth of all companies that increased employment did so through temporary contracts.
CONSUMER GOODS

Production of consumer goods rose sharply during September in response to rapid growth in new orders (the Output Index reached the highest level since October 1994). The main source of new orders was the UK, rather than overseas markets. The amount of goods purchased for use in production also showed strong growth, but the prices paid for these goods fell again and delivery times were on the whole marginally faster compared with a month ago. These factors suggest that supply bottlenecks and inflationary pressures were not present despite the increase in output. Producers allowed stocks of finished goods to rise to meet forecast demand, but the weak Employment Index reflected a reluctance among many firms to take on additional staff.
INVESTMENT/CAPITAL

Producers of investment (capital) goods reported the first significant monthly increase in new orders for over a year in September. Demand from domestic and export markets was found to have strengthened, prompting an increase in output. The Output Index rose to its highest level since May last year and the New Orders Index to its highest since August last year. The increase in output led to the first monthly rise in the past year in the quantity of items purchased by investment goods producers. Prices paid for these goods were generally found to have fallen again while lead times were unchanged, reflecting the weakness of demand by historical standards. This weakness continued to affect employment levels as redundancies almost matched new recruits.
INTERMEDIATE GOODS

The Output Index for intermediate goods rose to its highest level since November 1994, the fourth consecutive monthly increase following a poor first half to the year. Growth in new orders remained strong but has slipped somewhat since July. This was largely due to ongoing slow growth in many export markets -- notably European. Weak export demand has been offset, however, by continued strong demand for components from UK manufacturers of consumer goods.

Firms generally increased the quantity of goods purchased to meet output growth and the prices paid for these purchases fell again -- although the Prices Index appears to have bottomed out in July. Delivery times showed their first lengthening since August 1995.
